text: Kristen Nygaard (27 August 1926 – 10 August 2002) was a Norwegian computer scientist, programming language pioneer, and politician. He is internationally recognized as the co-inventor of object-oriented programming and the programming language Simula, developed with Ole-Johan Dahl in the 1960s. Nygaard and Dahl were awarded the 2001 A. M. Turing Award for their contributions to computer science. Born in Oslo, he earned his master's degree in mathematics from the University of Oslo in 1956, with a thesis titled "Theoretical Aspects of Monte Carlo methods." From 1948 to 1960, he worked full-time at the Norwegian Defense Research Establishment, initially in computing and programming (1948–1954) and later in operational research (1952–1960). From 1957 to 1960, he led the first operations research groups in the Norwegian defense establishment and co-founded the Norwegian Operational Research Society (1959–1964). In 1960, he joined the Norwegian Computing Center (NCC), where he helped establish it as a research institute, becoming Director of Research in 1962. Together with Dahl, he developed the foundational concepts of object-oriented programming—such as objects, classes, inheritance, virtual quantities, and multi-threaded (quasi-parallel) execution—through the Simula I (1961–1965) and Simula 67 (1965–1968) languages, which were extensions of ALGOL 60. In 2004, the Association Internationale pour les Technologies Objets (AITO) established the Dahl–Nygaard Prize, awarded annually at the ECOOP conference to two individuals—senior and junior—making significant technical contributions to object-orientation in the spirit of Dahl and Nygaard’s pioneering work. Nygaard conducted research on planning, control, and data processing for Norwegian trade unions (1971–1973) with Olav Terje Bergo, and explored the social impact of computer technology and the general system description language DELTA (1973–1975) with Erik Holbaek-Hanssen and Petter Haandlykken. He served as professor at Aarhus University, Denmark (1975–1976), and became professor emeritus at the University of Oslo (part-time from 1977, full-time 1984–1996), contributing to the development of the Scandinavian School in System Development and participatory design. Starting in 1976, he co-developed and implemented the general object-oriented programming language BETA with Bent Bruun Kristensen, Ole Lehrmann Madsen, and Birger Møller-Pedersen, which is now available on many computer platforms. From 1976 to the 1980s, he chaired the steering committee of the Scandinavian research program System Development and Profession Oriented Languages (SYDPOL) and led the Cost-13 (European Common Market Commission)-financed project on extending profession-oriented languages for professional work involving artificial intelligence and information technology. From 1995 to 1999, his research focused on distributed systems, particularly as leader of the General Object-Oriented Distributed Systems (GOODS) project (1997–1999), funded by the Norwegian Research Council, which aimed to enhance object-oriented languages and system development methods by introducing concepts to describe relationships between layered or distributed programs and hardware and human users. The GOODS team included Haakon Bryhni, Dag Sjøberg, and Ole Smørdal. His final research interests were in introductory programming education and creating a process-oriented conceptual platform for informatics, leading to the development of the Comprehensive Object-Oriented Learning (COOL) project with international test sites. He delivered lectures and courses on these topics in Norway and abroad. In November 1999, he became chair of an advisory committee on Broadband Communication for the Norwegian Department for Municipal and Regional Affairs. From 2001, he held a part-time position at the Simula Research Laboratory. In June 1990, he received an honorary doctorate from Lund University, Sweden, and in June 1991, became the first individual to receive an honorary doctorate from Aalborg University, Denmark. He was elected a member of the Norwegian Academy of Sciences. In October 1990, he was awarded the Norbert Wiener Award for Social and Professional Responsibility by Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility. In 1999, he and Dahl received the Rosing Prize from the Norwegian Data Association for exceptional professional achievements. In June 2000, he was awarded an Honorary Fellowship by the Object Management Group for "his originating of object technology concepts." In November 2001, the IEEE awarded Nygaard and Dahl the IEEE John von Neumann Medal "For the introduction of the concepts underlying object-oriented programming through the design and implementation of Simula 67." In February 2002, they received the 2001 A. M. Turing Award from the Association for Computing Machinery, cited for "ideas fundamental to the emergence of object-oriented programming, through their design of the programming languages Simula I and Simula 67." In August 2000, he was made Commander of the Royal Norwegian Order of St. Olav by King Harald V. From 1971 to 2001, he was a member of the Labour Party and participated in its research policy committees. In 1984 and 1985, he chaired the Informatics Committee of the University of Oslo and contributed to the university’s plan for research, education, and computing and communication facilities. He was the first chairman of the Environment Protection Committee of the Norwegian Association for the Protection of Nature. He served as Norwegian representative in OECD activities on information technology for ten years in the 1970s and was a member of the Research Committee of the Norwegian Federation of Trade Unions, collaborating with unions globally. For several years, he managed an experimental social institution aimed at creating humane living conditions for socially outcast alcoholics. Nygaard was active in Norwegian politics, serving on the National Executive Committee of the Norwegian Liberal Party in the mid- and late-1960s and as chair of its Strategy Committee. He was a minor ballot candidate in the 1949 parliamentary election. During the 1972 referendum on Norway’s membership in the European Common Market (later the European Union), he coordinated youth organizations opposing membership. From 1971 to 2001, he was a Labour Party member and involved in research policy committees. In November 1988, he became chair of the Information Committee on Norway and the EEC, which was reorganized in August 1990 as Nei til EF, an organization focused on informing the public about Norway’s relationship with the Common Market and advocating against membership. In 1993, following the EEC’s ratification of the Maastricht Treaty and the formation of the European Union, the organization changed its name to reflect this. Nei til EF became the largest political organization in Norway (145,000 members in 1994, from a population of 4 million). Nygaard worked with Anne Enger Lahnstein, leader of the anti-EU Centre Party, in this campaign. In the 28 November 1994 referendum, "Nei til EU" won with 52.2% of the vote and the highest voter participation in Norwegian history: 88.8%. Nygaard’s strategy emphasized advocating for something in addition to opposition, specifically the Scandinavian welfare state, which he viewed as threatened by the Maastricht Agreement. He resigned as chair in 1995 and later served on the organization’s strategy committee and council. In 1996 and 1997, he coordinated efforts to establish the European Anti-Maastricht Movement (TEAM), a cooperative network of national organizations opposing the Economic and Monetary Union and the Maastricht Treaty, which was successfully launched on 3 March 1997. Nygaard married Johanna Nygaard in 1951; she worked at the Norwegian Agency for Aid to Developing Countries, specializing in recruiting and administrative support for specialists in East Africa. They had three children and seven grandchildren. Nygaard died of a heart attack in 2002.
